item.title: Haley Stevens' Democratic allies turn on her after surprise GOP endorsement
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Michigan, speaks alongside Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers after a church service at Perfecting Church, in Detroit on Sunday, November 1, 2026. - Jose Juarez/AP As recently as Saturday night, the prospect of Democrat Haley Stevens endorsing Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan’s Senate race had seemed implausible. Stevens issued a statement praising Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed for saying he disagreed with a controversial advertisement that blamed the high cost of living in Michigan on the United States’ aid to Israel. Despite a week of speculation about her withdrawing an endorsement for El-Sayed, her primary rival, she repeatedly said that she would do no such thing. When staffers reached out last week to urge her not to endorse Rogers, Stevens replied in a text message, according to a person who saw the message: “Omg why would you think I would do that??!!” At midnight Saturday, she told a key ally that she was sticking with El-Sayed. Then on Sunday morning, things changed. She appeared at a Black church in Detroit with Rogers and then announced her change of heart to reporters gathered outside and on social media. Her move stunned the political world — including Stevens’ friends, colleagues and even her own congressional staffers, most of whom found out about her decision on social media and promptly quit, according to a statement from her chief of staff and people familiar with the matter. The question that could decide Michigan’s Senate race — and potentially, with it, which party will have majority control of the chamber for the last two years of Donald Trump’s presidency — is whether Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers will change votes or amount to more than political melodrama. There have long been signs of discontent with El-Sayed within the Democratic coalition. Stevens was strongest in the August primary with Black and Jewish Democrats, some of whom have balked at supporting El-Sayed, a Muslim who is a strident critic of Israel’s actions in Gaza and an advocate for ending foreign aid for Israel’s military. Prior to Stevens’ defection, CNN’s most recent poll of the Michigan Senate race had El-Sayed leading Rogers by seven points – with 95% support from Democratic likely voters. Already, Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers is becoming something of a rally-around-the-flag moment for Democratic leaders — uniting a coalition in the race’s final days around a shared sense of the stakes at hand. Among the Democratic leaders who denounced Stevens and strongly backed El-Sayed were two of his most powerful intra-party critics: Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, who tacitly supported Stevens in the primary, and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, who just days ago said El-Sayed’s views on Israel were “wrong” and “more than concerning.” Schumer accused Stevens of a “despicable betrayal.” “Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors,” the New York Democrat said . Schumer added that Democrats “are equally united in our total revulsion at the racist, Islamophobic, and over-the-top false attacks on Abdul by Republicans.” Pelosi, meanwhile, said on social media that El-Sayed “must win,” and that Stevens “has chosen to dangerously betray Michigan families’ healthcare, freedoms and future with her horrific endorsement of Mike Rogers.” As Stevens and Rogers spoke to reporters outside the church after the service, an individual in the crowd shouted: “Haley’s a traitor!” An El-Sayed campaign spokesperson said he raised $2.4 million on Sunday after Stevens endorsed Rogers — marking his “biggest fundraising day yet.” What Stevens said on CNN In an interview Sunday night with CNN’s Anderson Cooper, Stevens said that endorsing Rogers was “just a weight off my shoulders.” But she struggled to answer questions about why she’d changed her mind. “Abdul has been getting angrier and angrier,” Stevens said. “There are so many Democrats who want to vote for our Democratic nominee, and they’re just being told, ‘Hey, this is a party you don’t belong in, or this is a campaign you don’t belong in.’” What she didn’t explain, despite being asked several times, was what had changed between Saturday — when she told several Democrats she intended to appear with El-Sayed and Clyburn at church — and Sunday morning, when she instead went to a Detroit church with Rogers and endorsed him. She said she was tired of watching El-Sayed stand with Hasan Piker — but didn’t address the reality that El-Sayed’s campaign appearances with Piker came before the primary election, and Stevens had endorsed El-Sayed after that primary’s conclusion. “I’m just sick of the people he stands with,” Stevens said. Michigan Rep. Debbie Dingell, a Democrat who had told CNN Sunday that Stevens reassured her Saturday that she wasn’t switching sides, reacted by saying: “That was one of the most painful interviews I have ever watched.” Why did Stevens switch her endorsement? Shortly after their primary, which El-Sayed won by less than a percentage point, the two hugged at a state party unity breakfast. But they had not campaigned together in months – or spoken directly during that time, as CNN reported last week. Democrats attempted to negotiate a joint appearance Sunday at a Black church in Detroit alongside South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn, one of the party’s most influential figures. The goal was to shore up Black support for El-Sayed. One longtime Michigan Democratic operative said many older Black voters tend to cast their ballots on Election Day, rather than voting early, “because of a well-earned higher skepticism of absentee voting.” Those votes could be an essential piece of the Democratic coalition El-Sayed is trying to hold together. Stevens said in a statement Friday morning that Clyburn, who endorsed and campaigned with her in the primary, had invited her to the church — and that she would be attending, marking the first time she would appear jointly with El-Sayed on the campaign trail. However, she also issued a list of demands for El-Sayed — including attempting to pressure him into denouncing an outside group’s new advertisement that blamed the United States’ foreign aid for Israel for Americans’ struggles with high costs. The ad features two people in a grocery store suggesting they can’t afford basic goods due to the aid. It echoed what El-Sayed has often said on the campaign trail about Israel, even as he distanced himself from the ad. El-Sayed responded in a statement Friday night that Stevens “seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago.” It became clear that the joint appearance wouldn’t happen late Friday, when CNN and other outlets reported that El-Sayed’s campaign had asked Stevens to skip all campaign events in the race’s closing days. Dingell said on CNN Saturday that she was the one who delivered the message to Stevens. Still, on Saturday, El-Sayed denounced the ad, and Stevens issued a statement praising him for doing so — developments that made her decision Sunday more of a head-scratcher to many Democrats close to her. Dingell told CNN Sunday that Stevens had reassured her overnight that she wasn’t switching sides. Standing next to Rogers on Sunday, Stevens mentioned four times that El-Sayed’s campaign had excluded her from his events. She pointed to it again in her endorsement video posted on X, noting El-Sayed “had said that I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away. And he’s right.” “My vote for Senate is going to be with Mike Rogers, and I will tell you why. Because we have to stand with country. We can’t stand with hate. We can’t stand with Hasan Piker,” she said. Party officials moved swiftly on Sunday to publicly condemn Stevens and criticize her focus on being uninvited. But they privately said there was blame to go around — notably for El-Sayed. “He acted like he won the primary in a landslide, but he didn’t,” one longtime Democratic official told CNN. “Abdul gave himself his own October surprise.” El-Sayed went ahead Sunday with the event. After asking reporters to focus on questions about issues facing people in his state rather than “two folks who aren’t here right now,” El-Sayed was asked if he believed Stevens had betrayed his party by backing Rogers. “At the end of the day, I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens,” he said, standing next to Clyburn. “I think about, like I said, the 9,999,998 people who are not those two. Because you know what? I’m just less interested in the politics of it all than I am in the policy of it all.” Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed attends a church service at Greater Emmanuel Institutional Church of God in Christ, Sunday, November 1, 2026, in Detroit. - Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP A core tension in Michigan reemerges A deeply emotional argument for many in the Democratic Party became particularly personal for El-Sayed and Stevens, both of whom are known for not listening much to advisers and following their own instincts. Stevens was backed in the primary by tens of millions of dollars in spending from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee — a flashpoint between her and El-Sayed, who denounced AIPAC and the influence of money in politics at nearly every campaign event. El-Sayed was criticized for campaigning with Piker, the stridently pro-Palestinian live-streamer with a long history of controversial comments about Jews, including comparing Jewish residents who oppose El-Sayed to members of the Ku Klux Klan, remarks widely denounced as antisemitic. AIPAC on X reshared Stevens’ video on Sunday endorsing Rogers. During the primary, El-Sayed portrayed Stevens as an AIPAC puppet and called her “the least capable candidate in America.” “Everyone in America understands you want to blame all of your problems on Jewish Americans,” Stevens responded on X days before the August 4 election . As AIPAC’s allied groups boosted her campaign, the animosity grew too. El-Sayed’s multiple shots at Stevens as being a puppet angered her and made her dig in. Meanwhile, she was rankled by his repeated refusal to affirm that Israel had a right to exist as a Jewish state and his statements that it was committing genocide in Gaza and that funding to the country was hurting Michiganders. Many of Stevens’ Democratic critics on Sunday blamed Stevens’ fiancé, Michigan lawyer Jason Turkish, who endorsed Rogers last week and did media interviews criticizing El-Sayed as uncommitted to Jewish safety. One former Stevens staffer noted Sunday that after she and Turkish became engaged in May — something they kept private until after the August primary — Stevens grew more focused on defending Israel and AIPAC, even as the Democratic Party and US public opinion as a whole has become more skeptical of Israel. In the ex-staffer’s view, she was speaking less about the message she’d run on and won with before: growing Michigan’s economy and protecting manufacturing. The topic often came up while preparing for interviews or donor calls, the staffer said. Preparing for a June interview, Stevens pressed aides on why she should avoid defending AIPAC when she had done so in a 2022 House primary against former Rep. Andy Levin and won. Speculation about Turkish’s influence burst into the open on Sunday, as Democrats — many of whom had either spoken to Stevens recently or been briefed by people who had — suggested he was playing an outsized role for a candidate’s partner. Former Pennsylvania Rep. Susan Wild, who in 2023 was Stevens’ roommate in Washington and whose children regularly text with Stevens, said she was “terribly sad and disappointed” by her friend’s “appalling” move. “If this is because of her new relationship (about which many of us were so happy for her after she lost the primary), all I can say is that any woman who abandons her friends when a new guy comes along is no friend at all,” Wild said. Stevens’ mother, Maria Marcotte, a retired advertising executive, told CNN in a statement that her daughter’s fiancé had nothing to do with the change of heart — and that Marcotte herself had also voted for Rogers. “Haley is her own woman. She always has been. Suggesting a man made her decision for her is insulting to her, and it is insulting to me as her mother,” Marcotte said. She pointed to episodes in which progressive pro-Palestinian activists hounded Stevens during the primary campaign. “Abdul should not have thrown her out of the campaign for speaking her truth,” she said. “Haley made this choice herself, with her eyes open, the way she has made every hard choice in her life. And I know Haley will support whoever wins this election, because that is who she is. I have never been prouder of her.” Who’s to blame? The anger between the two rivals kept growing from a distance after El-Sayed won the primary. El-Sayed grouped Stevens in with all those he decided he didn’t need to build his coalition after his primary victory. Stevens would tell people that she thought he was running a weird and losing campaign, but that she didn’t feel it was her obligation to fix it. Rogers aides, aware that his path to victory largely depended on a Democratic civil war, restrained themselves to spreading word of discontent and convincing themselves they weren’t just fantasizing that they could get her all the way to endorsing. Then came the grocery-store ad that rekindled the tension. It was released by a group linked to Cenk Uygur, co-creator of The Young Turks and — in a twist practically designed to create acrimony — Piker’s uncle. As Stevens demanded he denounce Uygur’s ad, El-Sayed returned to name-checking AIPAC in his statement criticizing Stevens, something Michigan attorney general Dana Nessel, a Stevens primary backer who has raised concerns about Jewish safety, asked him to stop doing before she endorsed him. Nessel told CNN in October that El-Sayed had agreed to her request. Stevens’ defection threatened to worsen El-Sayed’s standing with Jewish voters. Rogers has already predicted publicly that he could win as much as half the Jewish vote on Tuesday. “It feels like over the last eight weeks, Dr. El-Sayed has become more egregious in the language he’s been using,” said Rabbi Aaron Starr, the president of the Michigan Board of Rabbis and a leader of the “Nonnegotiable” group of Jewish leaders. That group calls on El-Sayed to do more about concerns regarding Jewish safety and to affirm Jewish sovereignty in Israel. Starr and other Jewish leaders held a call Sunday afternoon to discuss the endorsement flip. But Stevens was also damaged with key allies. Dingell, long a peacemaker within the state party, chided Stevens’ “continued efforts to get attention.” “Unfortunately, she’s seriously hurt herself,” Dingell told CNN. Curtis Hertel, the chairman of the Michigan Democratic Party, effectively booted Stevens from it. He wrote on social media: “Congresswoman Stevens is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future.” Many Democrats in the state felt that for most of the preceding year, Stevens was viable in the Senate race largely because she’d cornered Schumer into effectively backing her. Into the spring, complaints circulated about what a lackluster primary campaign she was running, how much she was struggling on the stump, and how she was lashing out against those who wouldn’t support her. Despite her eventual strength with African American voters, Black church leaders were angry about her efforts to push for early endorsements. Chokwe Pitchford, a 27-year-old district commissioner from Benton Harbor and seen as a local rising star, told a story that he says encapsulated the kind of experience other Michigan Democrats he knows had: One morning, he discovered a graphic online from Stevens saying he’d endorsed her, even though as he posted in response, they’d never spoken. “Instead of reaching out and apologizing, I had people from around the state calling from unknown numbers saying my political career is over if I don’t take that down,” Pitchford told CNN. “Some of us tried to ring this alarm bell a year ago; there was a problem here.” Indeed, the most robust praise for Stevens on Sunday was coming from Republicans. “Haley said what few people are willing to say. She showed great and almost unprecedented loyalty to the Great People of Michigan with what she did,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. The story and headline have been updated with additional information. Todd reported from Detroit. CNN’s Dana Bash, Manu Raju, Nicky Robertson and Jeff Zeleny contributed to this report. For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/01/politics/haley-stevens-abdul-el-sayed-mike-rogers-michigan-primary-what-happened

item.title: Early voting is breaking records, but the numbers tell a complicated story
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
On the eve of Election Day a record number of Americans have already passed judgement on President Donald Trump and the Republican-controlled Congress. Roughly 54 million voters cast their early ballots over this past weekend ahead of the Nov. 3 election, according to the University of Florida Election Lab . The deluge offers a glimpse into a forecasted wave election that many experts believe could sweep Democrats in power for the president's final two years in the White House. Every state has different rules on compiling voters' age, race or party affiliation with some providing no demographic statistics at all. But it does reveal important voter behavior and some demographics that paint a clearer picture about who is more motivated in the 2026 midterms. Michael McDonald, a political science professor who runs the Election Lab, said the initial outlook indicates a younger, more diverse and politically independent electorate is showing up. "I can confidently say that the 2026 election will be the most diverse midterm electorate in U.S. history," in an Oct. 28 post on X. But the data alone, much like the various polls , cannot predict the outcome of who will be in charge of the House and Senate next year, McDonald and others have warned. Here's a look at the big takeaways from the early voting totals. A lot more people are showing up than in 2022 For starters, 8 million more people took advantage of the early in-person and mail-in ballot options over the weekend than during the last 2022 midterms, which gave Republicans control of the House during former President Joe Biden 's term. Political observers are marveling at those numbers and note how they surged in places with more competitive Senate contests, such as Ohio, Maine and Michigan. In Texas, Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton have locked horns in arguably the most watched race of this year's cycle. The early totals show more than 7.7 million people have cast early ballots, which surpasses the Lone Star State's high mark of 40% turnout during the 2018 midterms. "Their record for a midterm election is 8.3 million total. So they're just over about 600,000 or so ballots away from their highest turnout ever... Election Day hasn't even happened yet. That's remarkable," David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, said during CBS' Face the Nation on Nov. 1. Same goes for Georgia, where more than 2.8 million voters have showed up already representing a 13% increase compared to 2022; Michigan with more than 2.3 million marking a 26% increase; and South Carolina where about 1.1 million have shown up compared to approximately 620,000 four years ago which is a whomping 75% increase. Records were also broken in North Carolina, where Democrats are hoping former Gov. Roy Cooper can flip a GOP-held Senate seat against former RNC Chair Michael Whatley. The Tar Heel State began sending out early voting mail-in ballots Oct. 15 and combined with in-person about 2.8 million have reportedly showed up already. That is a 31% increase compared to the midterm election four years ago, Western Carolina University political scientist Chris Cooper said in an Oct. 31 post on Substack . "Voter turnout was higher on every day of early voting than on the comparable day in 2022," he said. 'Bloodbath': Democrats, independents turnout is up while GOP is down Far more Democrats than Republicans made their voices heard in the early voting process with some states outpacing their 2024 presidential totals, the preliminary data show. Of the 54 million ballots cast, about 43% were from Democrats and 32% were from GOP voters, with the about 25% coming from independent or "unaffiliated" voters. Keep in mind that these statistics are limited to the 27 states that report party affiliation. It also reflects the voter's registration rather than their exact choice on the ballot. But some Republicans are already expressing nervousness about the low GOP turnout , especially given Trump's unpopularity among those showing up more. An AP-NORC poll released Oct. 8, for example, found 25% of U.S. adults approve of his handling of the economy, with just 9% of Democrats and 23% of independents agreeing. "I am deeply, deeply worried. What we're seeing across the country is massive Democrat turnout," Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, during an Oct. 30 episode of "The Verdict," his podcast. "Democrats are showing up. They are energized. They hate, hate, hate Donald Trump. If the election were over today, if just the early votes that have been cast so far were counted, Republicans would lose massively. It would not be close. We would lose both the House and Senate. It would be a bloodbath." For the past several weeks Trump and his allies have been zig-zagging across the nation, focusing heavily on conservative strongholds in order to motivate their base. He is set to speak at the Reflecting Pool in Washington, D.C., capping off a blitz of last-minute appearances in states where Republicans face competitive challengers. GOP voters historically have swarmed Election Day when tens of millions of Americans will likely to flock the polls as well, but experts say the early voting patterns mirror past trends. "It would be highly unusual for Election Day to be dramatically different than in the past, so I would not hold out hope for a huge Republican wave to make up for their in-person early voting deficit where we are seeing a lack of Republican early voting engagement," McDonald said on his Substack. Racially diverse and younger voters fueling turnout The United States is becoming a more racially and ethnically diverse nation, and that's showing up in our elections as a higher percentage of Black and Hispanic voters make up the electorate. Of the handful of states that submit race and ethnicity information from early voting totals there is a noteworthy uptick among voters of color, while voting among White people lags behind and remains similar to 2022 levels. Hispanic turnout in Texas is especially noteworthy given it has exceeded the 2024 presidential levels , fueled largely by younger voters, Tom Bonier, a Democratic data and polling expert, told USA TODAY in an October interview. In the state's predominantly Hispanic counties, analysts say they are finding turnout to be higher than the statewide average. Trump and the GOP will need to hold their gains among Hispanic voters , who helped fuel his 2024 victory but has soured on the administration especially over its strict immigration enforcement campaign. The Pew Research Center found Trump's approval among Hispanic voters sits at 24% , which is down from 38% in February 2025. Among Black voters, who make up a larger share of the South electorate, there is reported anger of Trump's redistricting war that carved up many majority-Black congressional districts. That is could help to fuel a surge being seen in southern states such as Georgia, North Carolina and South Carolina, where there's a Senate race surprisingly within the margin of error . The Election Lab shows Black early voting accounts for about 32% of Georgia's turnout thus far, which is about three percentage points better than during the 2022 midterm. Even that small jump, however, can be significant given the Peach State's toss-up status, particularly in its closely watched race for governor between Democrat Keisha Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor, and Republican Keith Jackson, a healthcare CEO. In South Carolina, for instance, the numbers show Black voters making up about 27% of the electorate which is significantly higher than in past cycles overall. McDonald said by all indicators this midterm should be a good one for Democrats and that figures coming from these states show elevated engagement from those demographics. "Since the Democratic coalition is more diverse, their higher engagement levels will yield a more diverse electorate," he said. This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: What early voting does and doesn’t tell us about the 2026 midterms This article originally appeared on USA TODAY at https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/elections/2026/11/02/early-voting-data-2026-midterm-elections/92562865007/

item.title: U.S. strikes Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz on eve of midterms
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — The United States has conducted defensive strikes on some Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz, a U.S. official said Monday, on the eve of crucial midterm elections . Iranian state television reported that explosions were heard on Qeshm Island. The official, who wasn’t authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity, said that “Iranians using surface to air missiles against U.S. assets” had been targeted. The strikes appeared to be limited as opposed to a return to full hostilities but followed President Donald Trump previously saying the U.S. would not launch new strikes on Iran before Tuesday's midterms. The unpopular war and the resulting impact on U.S. gasoline prices and other parts of the economy have been a vulnerability for Republicans as they try to keep control of Congress. The region is on edge about the prospects of the U.S. resuming full-scale operations against Iran, and the new strikes, which were reported earlier by The Wall Street Journal, are certain to raise fresh concerns. Backchannel negotiations also are playing out as Israel and some Middle East allies lobby Trump on the way ahead in the more than 8-month-old war that’s rattled global markets and wreaked havoc on Iran. The Trump administration was last known to have carried out attacks in early September , but thousands of U.S. troops remain in the waters off Iran to maintain a naval blockade aimed at preventing tankers hauling Iranian oil from getting to the global market. Plus, a third aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are on their way to the Middle East. Before the strikes were confirmed, U.S. Vice President JD Vance offered measured optimism that a deal could still be struck. Vance sent a letter to Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, last week, but the White House has offered scant details. Trump told reporters that letter was focused on assisting Iran with “medical supplies and various things.” “We’ve had a number of good conversations with the Iranians,” Vance told reporters Monday when asked about the letter. “I actually just spoke with the president of the United States about an hour ago about this. Look, the president and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement. We’re going to keep on working at it.” Netanyahu pushed Trump for strikes in a weekend call Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pushed for another wave of strikes on Iran after the U.S. elections , according to two regional officials and a third person familiar with the matter. A return to full-scale war with Iran could help Netanyahu to form an emergency government after he and his far-right allies lost their parliamentary majority in last week's elections. Trump has alternated between threatening major strikes and pushing for a deal with Iran. The two officials said diplomatic efforts have made progress, with Qatari mediators holding two rounds of talks last week with Iranian officials. The two officials said the mediators are trying to advance a framework for Iran to cease its attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in return for the U.S. lifting its blockade on Iran's ports. They said more talks are planned for this week. The two officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were discussing classified briefings they had received from American, and in one case Israeli, officials. One official said Netanyahu was working with senior officials in the U.S. administration to persuade Trump to launch a quick but extensive air campaign and that the president does not appear to have made a decision. Netanyahu pressed for strikes during a call over the weekend with Trump, who would not commit to taking military action, according to a person who was briefed on it. Other U.S. allies in the Middle East are warning against more strikes, saying that would destabilize the region and could lead Iran-allied Houthi rebels in Yemen to step up their attacks on Saudi Arabia and Red Sea shipping, a third regional official said. Iran-backed militias in Iraq could also get involved . The Israeli government did not immediately comment. The White House did not directly respond to questions about Netanyahu and Trump’s discussion of potential new strikes during the weekend call. Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman said he spoke by phone Monday with U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth about “the latest regional and international developments” and the Houthis’ continued attacks on Saudi Arabia. Trump downplays scale of Iran conflict Oil prices dropped sharply Monday as renewed diplomatic efforts in the Iran war appeared to show signs of headway. Trump noted the drop in a speech in Washington on Monday, which was billed as his closing argument to Americans, and sought to minimize the scale of the conflict, which has cost U.S. taxpayers at least $47 billion. “I don’t know if you even call it a war, because we haven’t been doing any fighting for months,” Trump said. Iran says it is prepared for war while pursuing diplomacy Iran wants guarantees that the U.S. will implement its side of any agreement. The U.S. and Israel have twice attacked Iran while it was engaged in negotiations over its disputed nuclear program. Iranian officials say publicly they are prepared for war or diplomacy. The new supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei , met with Iran’s military chiefs and said the response to “any kind and level of threat” from the U.S. or Israel should be immediate and without “geographic limits,” urging an expansion of the list of potential targets. A recent analysis by The Associated Press found that Iranian strikes on more than two dozen U.S. bases since the start of the war have caused billions of dollars in equipment damage. Rezaei, the Iranian security chief, told state television that “the tone has completely changed” from the U.S. and called it a “very good sign.” He gave no details about the letter from Vance and said he had not responded. Arab allies are caught in the middle October saw the most attacks on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz since March, as Iran has tried to ramp up economic pressure on the U.S. to get it to lift its blockade. The mood was grim at the Manama Dialogue, an annual security summit in Bahrain organized by the International Institute for Strategic Studies. United Arab Emirates presidential adviser Anwar Gargash told attendees the U.S. and Iranian stances are far apart, and “if these positions are not bridged, then we have to worry about the worst.” Gulf nations have spent billions of dollars to boost their defense capabilities since the war began. Egypt’s Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty told the gathering in Bahrain that the next escalation “will be more dangerous, more destructive, and it will lead to nowhere.” China will send a special envoy to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia in early to mid-November, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters Monday. ___ Magdy reported from New York, and Anna from Jerusalem. Victoria Eastwood in Cairo, Kanis Leung in Hong Kong and Katie Marie Davies in London contributed to this report. ___ AP STANDARDS: The AP uses anonymous sources only when the information is vital to the news report and not opinion or speculation. The information must be unavailable except under the conditions of anonymity imposed by the source. The source must be reliable, in a position to have accurate information and approved by news managers. item.title: Trump put himself on the midterms ballot without running. Now his legacy is at stake.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Trump’s political capital is on the line ahead of the midterm elections as a potential blue wave threatens his final two years in office. Trump has crisscrossed the country, holding 28 in-person campaign rallies in addition to a series of tele-rallies. The president has made stops in Republican strongholds like Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas and even Alaska in an effort to keep the states firmly in the red column. He’s also visited a number of deep-red states like Mississippi and South Carolina, where polls show closer than expected races. While Trump has argued his rallies have boosted Republican incumbents and candidates in the states, recent polling suggests otherwise. A New York Times/Siena poll released the day before Election Day showed Democrats with leads in Senate races in Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas and Alaska. Trump’s heavy political investment in the states means he could end up shouldering the blame for a potential blue wave, which could impact the GOP beyond Election Day. Republicans warn that a blue wave would be detrimental to the last two years of the Trump administration, and by extension, his legacy. “It impacts his ability to drive policy over the next two years, or if a Supreme Court nomination comes up, or fill in the blank in terms of even Cabinet turnover,” said one Republican strategist, speaking on condition of anonymity. “All of that too will help shape his legacy, and it’s how people remember you at the end that guides you into the history books.” In a statement to The Hill on Monday, the Republican National Committee (RNC) warned that Democrats would “obstruct” Trump’s agenda and that their “disastrous economic policies” would drive jobs overseas. “The president knows what’s at stake this cycle, which is why he’s barnstormed the country to encourage our voters to support Republican candidates that will advance his agenda and deliver for the American people,” said RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre. But during an election eve speech at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, Trump did not appear entirely focused on the elections that could impact the trajectory of his last two years in office. The president spent the first 22 minutes of his 37-minute address — largely viewed as a closing message before the midterms — talking about his administration’s efforts to repair the Reflecting Pool. Trump showed off a number of pre-renovation pictures of the pool and at one point invited Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to the podium to give brief remarks. Trump also touted his numerous beautification projects and lower crime in the nation’s capital. Republican operative Rob Stutzman called Trump’s speech “another Captain Queeg moment,” a reference to a character from Herman Wouk’s 1951 novel “The Caine Mutiny” who is considered an unstable and incompetent commander. A second Republican strategist said, “What the utter f--- was that?” when asked for their reaction to Trump’s speech at the Reflecting Pool. “Republicans were hoping that he would have some sort of a closing message, some sort of American message with it, with a wonderful backdrop that could maybe be of help in the closing hours here,” the unnamed GOP strategist said. “As we Republicans are losing touch with the public, it looked like he was losing touch with reality.” One national Republican operative noted the speech was “not surprising” considering Trump’s communication style but expressed frustration with the closing message. “This perfectly encapsulates his messaging throughout this entire campaign cycle, but it’s deeply frustrating when we need to be laser-focused on turning out our low propensity voters tomorrow,” the operative said. A third Republican strategist defended the speech, arguing the Reflecting Pool was “a hook” for Trump to be able to talk about issues like crime and immigration. “It’s one of these things that wherever you get the opportunity to speak to a national audience, you’re going to talk about the midterms even if you have to start with something else,” the strategist said. Trump did take some time during his speech Monday to urge Republicans to turn out on Election Day. “If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” the president said. “Now, that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is — Republican or Democrat, good or bad, good president, great president, bad president — for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms.” “We gave this a very strong shot,” he added. Much of the GOP’s strategy has hinged on turning out its low-propensity base as much as possible, arguably a tall order for any political party in a nonpresidential election. Republicans hoped to defy that trend by dispatching Trump on the campaign trail, urging voters to “pretend” like he is on the ballot. “The amount of rallies he did shows he ‘believes’ that he’s on the ballot tomorrow,” said Dan Eberhart, a Republican donor. “He worked hard, and he’s right: Tomorrow’s outcome is a reflection on him.” In a statement to The Hill, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle referred to Trump as the GOP’s “best messenger” and “unmatched motivator” who is “committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress.” But some Republicans are unsure whether that tactic will ultimately work. “So far from what we’ve seen, those rallies have not done what they were meant to do,” said the first unnamed Republican strategist. Democrats have been heartened by signs of early turnout in key battlegrounds, but Republicans argue that a large share of their voters tend to vote in person on Election Day. “They’re banking on these Republicans and the folks that he’s trying to rally to show up tomorrow, and Republicans historically and should do exceedingly well tomorrow,” the first Republican strategist said. “But the fact is, they still underperformed in places like Texas and in Florida in the early vote.” According to data released by Texas’s secretary of State, 7.7 million voters in the Lone Star State voted early. Meanwhile in Florida, registered Republicans led registered Democrats in early voting by just a little more than 200,000 voters. By comparison, in 2022, registered Republicans led Democrats in early voting by just a little less than 500,000 voters. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) on Sunday sounded the alarm over low turnout in the state, which has become known as a nerve center for Republican politics. “If people stay home, you could end up seeing results that you’re going to be wondering what happened. That’s just the reality,” DeSantis said at a campaign event. “The reality is gas is higher, and that’s not good. Some of these Republicans act like it’s no big deal. I disagree with that. It is a big deal to people,” the Florida governor continued. Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. All rights reserved. This material may not be published, broadcast, rewritten, or redistributed. item.title: Supreme Court rejects Trump admin's bid to set aside thousands of California ballots
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Voters check in at a polling location in Los Angeles in June. (Kyle Grillot / Bloomberg via Getty) WASHINGTON — In a loss for President Donald Trump, the Supreme Court on Monday swiftly rejected the administration’s request that California separate out up to 20,000 mail-in ballots that officials allege could be submitted by noncitizens. In a brief order without explanation, the court turned away an emergency request the Trump administration filed just hours earlier in an unusual last-minute flurry of election litigation. Lower courts had also ruled against the Trump administration. The court acted so quickly that it did not even ask California for its views first, as it normally does of the opposing party in such cases. “This latest decision should put an end to the administration’s attempt to disrupt California’s elections through emergency court orders,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat, said in a statement. “But our work is not over. We will remain vigilant and keep fighting back against federal efforts to undermine our democracy,” he added. The White House and Justice Department did not immediately respond to requests seeking comment. California officials had resisted the Justice Department’s intervention, noting that it is already illegal under state law for noncitizens to vote and expressing skepticism about whether the federal government’s information is accurate. Separately, the administration has warned California election officials they could face prosecution if they allow noncitizens to vote. A federal judge told the Justice Department on Saturday to stop making such threats. Although elections are administered exclusively by local officials, the Trump administration says it has grounds to intervene because there is a federal law that prohibits voting by noncitizens. Trump has long claimed, without evidence, that millions of noncitizens illegally vote in U.S. elections. Experts say it rarely happens. That has not stopped the administration from putting pressure on states to check voters’ citizenship, including by using a federal database. But the effort has faced multiple setbacks. When the federal government said it had confirmed 185 noncitizens registered to vote in Nevada, the state responded that all of them were, in fact, citizens. Thousands of mail-in ballots have already been submitted and processed in California. Once election officials check whether a ballot is valid by checking the voter’s signature against voter registration records, the details identifying the voter are discarded before the vote is counted. As a result, it would be impossible to retroactively determine which votes may have been cast by the alleged noncitizens. In rejecting the Trump administration’s claims, the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals said there was no evidence Congress intended the federal law that bars noncitizens from voting to pre-empt state election laws. Travis Crum, an NBC News contributor and election law expert at Washington University in St. Louis, said the Supreme Court’s decisive action rejecting the Trump administration was similar to how it turned away a series of Republican requests seeking to use a new congressional district map over the summer. In both instances “the court acted quickly to show its displeasure for the underlying claims” as well as reinforcing longstanding precedent against federal courts intervening in elections when they are underway, Crum said. item.title: Prosecutors announce intention to retry Lindsay Clancy for deaths of her 3 children
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Prosecutors announced in court on Nov. 2 that they intend to retry Lindsay Clancy , the Massachusetts mother who killed her three young children. Clancy, 36, was charged with murder for killing her children Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, on Jan. 24, 2023, by strangling them with exercise bands in the basement of their Duxbury home. Clancy's attorney Kevin Reddington argued she can't be held criminally responsible, Massachusetts' version of the insanity defense, because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time of the killings. Clancy's triple murder trial ended with a hung jury in early September, leaving her fate in limbo. Plymouth County Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague said prosecutors want to retry Clancy but are waiting to decide what charges she will face until Judge William Sullivan makes a decision on three motions, including a defense motion to dismiss the murder charges. "Your honor, this would be a retrial. As to what that looks like will depend," Sprague said. "We're not at that point yet." Reddington argued prosecutors don't need to know the outcome of the motions to determine what charges they will retry Clancy on. "Why do we not know if the next trial will be murder in the first degree, or a lesser charge or no charge?" he asked. Reddington said he wants Sullivan, who is approaching mandatory retirement in June, to preside over the trial in the spring. Sullivan said requested the parties appear on Nov. 16 for another hearing. If Sullivan dismisses the defense's motion to dismiss at that hearing, the parties will then select a trial date, which Sullivan said he is hoping to schedule in March. Judge to weigh motion to dismiss The defense team pushed to have the charges against Clancy dismissed altogether and launch an investigation into the holdout juror. Defense attorney Martin Weinberg argued on Nov. 2 that retrying Clancy would violate constitutional protections against double jeopardy because Sullivan should have questioned the jury more thoroughly after receiving notes indicating one juror was refusing to follow the court's instruction on reasonable doubt, an allegation the holdout juror has denied . Sullivan interjected, noting he did question the jurors individually before declaring a mistrial on Sept. 4. Weinberg said the question Sullivan asked was “simply constitutionally insufficient to probe what was going on in that jury room." Prosecutors opposed the defense's motion , saying the mistrial was properly declared after the jury repeatedly reported it was deadlocked. Sprague argued that Sullivan could not have questioned the jurors further without probing the substance of deliberations, which is prohibited, and even if he could have done so, the appropriate response wouldn’t be dismissing the charges. "It’s not for the trial judge to choose sides in a deadlocked jury and decide," she said. Sullivan said he would take the matter under advisement. Defense argues for holdout juror probe Reddington also requested the holdout juror's phone, phone records and confidential questionnaire, among other records. Reddington asked the court to question the juror about the truthfulness of a questionnaire and his answers during jury selection, a "sworn assurance" from Sept. 3, and the use of a cell phone or receipt of outside information during deliberations. In a fiery exchange on Nov. 2, Reddington said he has evidence the holdout juror was using his cellphone and researching altruistic filicide during deliberations. Reddington said the juror was also dishonest about his criminal history on his questionnaire. Heather O'Connor, an attorney for the holdout juror, said that the mistrial decision had to be made based on what was known at the time and that these allegations came to light after the jury was dismissed. "And to be clear Juror Doe does not concede any of those allegations," O'Connor said. Sullivan said he would take the matter under advisement. Prosecutors push for gag order Prosecutors also asked the court to prohibit defense attorneys, as well as themselves, from speaking to the media in a way that would "have a substantial likelihood of materially prejudicing the criminal proceedings." Sprague argued Reddington has already made many statements that were inappropriate and "calculated to affect the public's perception of the case," including asking for a presidential pardon and saying the other jurors were "robbed" by the holdout. A defense attorney opposed that motion, arguing that such an order would constitute "prior restraint" of speech that infringes upon both Reddington's and Clancy's First Amendment rights. They said that no trial date had been set and the impact of these alleged comments on a potential future jury is "merely speculative." Sullivan said he would also take this matter under advisement.
